edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Session State patterns (Client/Server/Database Session State)
edges.note: Three mutually exclusive ways to hold session state; on the client vs in server memory.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Session State patterns
edges.note: State on the client sent per request vs committed to shared persistent store between requests.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Session State patterns
edges.note: In-server-memory session vs persisted-in-DB session; pick one to locate session state.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Web Presentation (Template View / Transform View)
edges.note: Two rival View strategies: fill markers in a static template vs programmatically transform each data element.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Two Step View
edges.note: Two Step View is commonly realized as two chained Transform View (e.g. XSLT) stages: logical page then formatting.
The second formatting stage of a Two Step View can be implemented with a Template View applying site appearance.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Web Presentation (Page Controller / Front Controller)
edges.note: Controller-per-page vs one handler for all requests; two rival input-controller structures.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Application Controller
edges.note: A Front Controller commonly delegates screen-navigation/action flow decisions to an Application Controller.

edges.cite: Fowler PoEAA, Page Controller
edges.note: A Page Controller handles the request then renders the response, typically via a Template View.
An Application Controller can drive flow above Page Controllers as well as a Front Controller.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.8 API Gateway
edges.note: Routing client requests to the correct backend is a core function the API Gateway performs.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.8 (API composition at the gateway)
edges.note: The gateway fans a request to several services and composes one response (API composition/aggregation).

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.8 API Gateway
edges.note: The gateway absorbs edge cross-cutting concerns (TLS, auth, rate limiting) offloaded from services.
A single gateway typically routes and aggregates together, so the two functions are deployed side by side.
Aggregating gateway also offloads TLS/auth for the composed calls; both run in the same edge component.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.8 (BFF variant); Azure BFF pattern
edges.note: BFF is an API Gateway variant: one purpose-built gateway per frontend type instead of a single shared one.

edges.cite: Azure Backends for Frontends pattern (related: Gateway Aggregation)
edges.note: Each BFF aggregates the specific backend calls its frontend needs into tailored responses.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.3/8 (service discovery)
edges.note: The gateway queries service discovery to find live instances before routing to them.
Offloading authentication at the gateway means delegating to a federated identity provider that issues tokens.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.3 (registry + health check)
edges.note: The registry polls or receives health-check results to deregister unhealthy instances.

edges.cite: Azure Health Endpoint Monitoring pattern
edges.note: The monitoring pattern (probing side) polls the liveness/readiness endpoints exposed by the Health Check API.

edges.cite: Azure Health Endpoint Monitoring pattern
edges.note: Load balancers consume health-endpoint probes to route traffic around unhealthy instances.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.11 (observability patterns)
edges.note: Sibling observability patterns used together; correlation/trace ids tie aggregated logs to traces.
A service mesh's sidecars inject and propagate trace context and emit spans, providing tracing transparently.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.4 (orchestration-based saga)
edges.note: An orchestration-based saga is coordinated by a central orchestrator, i.e. a process manager.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.4 (choreography-based saga)
edges.note: A choreography-based saga advances via services reacting to each other's events, no coordinator.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.4; EIP Process Manager
edges.note: Decentralized event choreography vs centralized orchestration: two ways to coordinate a multi-service workflow.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Routing Slip / Process Manager
edges.note: Precomputed itinerary carried on the message vs a central manager deciding each next step at runtime.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.3-4 (reliable messaging for sagas)
edges.note: Sagas need to atomically update state and emit saga commands/events; the outbox provides that reliability.

edges.cite: Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.3/6
edges.note: Two ways to atomically persist state and publish events: outbox table+relay vs deriving events from an event store.
Choreography is built on services publishing domain events that others subscribe and react to.

edges.cite: Azure Scheduler Agent Supervisor pattern ('Scheduler performs a similar function to the Process Manager')
edges.note: SAS is a resilient orchestration: a scheduler=process-manager plus a supervisor that recovers failed steps.

edges.cite: Azure Scheduler Agent Supervisor pattern (references Retry pattern)
edges.note: Agents implement retry logic to handle the transient faults SAS is designed to survive.

edges.cite: Azure Scheduler Agent Supervisor pattern (references Leader Election)
edges.note: Multiple supervisor instances use leader election so they don't compete to recover the same failed step.

edges.cite: Azure Scheduler Agent Supervisor pattern (references Compensating Transaction)
edges.note: When a step can't be recovered, the supervisor triggers compensating transactions to undo the whole task.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Messaging Bridge / Channel Adapter
edges.note: A Messaging Bridge is a Channel-Adapter variant that connects two messaging systems rather than an app.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Channel Adapter
edges.note: A Channel Adapter is a specialized Message Endpoint linking a non-messaging application to a channel.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Messaging Bridge
edges.note: A bridge is a set of connected channel pairs replicating messages between two messaging systems.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Competing Consumers
edges.note: Multiple consumers pull from one shared point-to-point Message Channel, each message going to exactly one.

edges.cite: Azure Competing Consumers pattern
edges.note: Competing consumers drain a leveling queue; buffering plus parallel consumers absorb load spikes.

edges.cite: Azure Sequential Convoy pattern (when ordering not needed, use Competing Consumers)
edges.note: Plain competing consumers scale but lose ordering; sequential convoy adds per-group FIFO at scaling cost.

edges.cite: Azure Sequential Convoy pattern (builds on queue buffering)
edges.note: Convoy builds on a leveling queue, adding session partitioning to keep FIFO within each category.

edges.cite: Hohpe & Woolf EIP, Control Bus
edges.note: Control Bus is a separate management Message Channel overlay carrying config/heartbeat/monitoring traffic.
Bridging model mismatch two ways: one shared canonical model vs pairwise isolating translation per context.
Channel adapters translate each application's native format to/from the shared canonical model on the bus.

edges.cite: Azure Strangler Fig pattern; Richardson 'Microservices Patterns' ch.13
edges.note: Incremental migration inserts an anti-corruption layer between the new system and the surviving legacy model.

edges.cite: Evans DDD, Context Map / Anticorruption Layer
edges.note: An ACL guards one bounded context from an upstream/legacy model, translating at the boundary.
The immediately-accepted request is queued and processed by competing consumers while the client polls status.
Accepting the request then queuing backend work levels load and lets the client poll a status endpoint.

edges.cite: Azure Valet Key pattern (example contrasts with Gateway Routing proxying)
edges.note: Direct token-scoped client access to storage vs proxying all data transfer through a gateway.
Valet-key tokens let clients upload/download blobs directly to the store that also serves static content.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, Security tactics (Detect Intrusion)
edges.note: An IDS packages the Detect Intrusion tactic: compare traffic/activity against known attack signatures.
Layered perimeter defense: the firewall filters/blocks while the IDS monitors what passes for attack patterns.
IDS sensors are commonly deployed to watch the DMZ segment between external and internal networks.
A secrets vault applies the Encrypt Data tactic to protect stored credentials and keys at rest.
Workloads authenticate to the vault via a managed/federated identity before it releases secrets.

edges.cite: Azure Index Table pattern (index tables speed queries over sharded data)
edges.note: Index tables map secondary keys to (hashed) shard keys so queries locate sharded data without full scans.
Both maintain precomputed read-optimized structures over a store to serve queries the base layout can't.

edges.cite: Azure Bulkhead pattern (related: Throttling)
edges.note: Throttling keeps each isolated compartment within its capacity so it can't exhaust its partition.

edges.cite: Azure Bulkhead pattern (related: Health Endpoint Monitoring)
edges.note: Health monitoring detects a failing compartment so traffic is kept out of it, preserving isolation.
Hanmer fault-tolerant ops: operators react to faults surfaced by the Fault Observer via a maintenance interface.
The Fault Observer publishes collected fault reports to loggers, i.e. into centralized log aggregation.
Both are out-of-band management channels distinct from application data; a control bus carries admin traffic.

edges.cite: Facebook Flux docs / overview (unidirectional data flow vs MVC)
edges.note: Flux was introduced as a strict one-way-dataflow alternative to bidirectional MVC for UI state.
Both are unidirectional UI architectures (Redux/Flux was inspired by Elm); a project picks one model.
The server renders the page from templates with placeholders where interactive islands are hydrated.
Everything outside the islands stays static HTML/assets that can be served from static hosting/CDN.
Cross-domain SSO is realized by delegating authentication to a trusted federated identity provider.
Itinerary-based routing is a form of message routing where the route rides on the message, not a central router.
